title: Adolf Franck in his book "La Kabbale"
content:
Adolf Franck in His Book "Kabbalah"

Adolf Franck's 1843 study constitutes a historiographic turning point, for he rescued Kabbalah from its status as a collection of superstitious beliefs and presented it as a rational and consistent philosophical system. Franck sought to prove that Jewish mysticism is not a late forgery but rather an ancient tradition possessing a profound philosophical core, which grants man a central and exalted role in the structure of the universe. Through comparative methodology, he identified the roots of Kabbalah in ancient Persian metaphysics, drawing parallels between the concepts of "Ein Sof" and the sefirot and Zoroastrian theology. Despite later criticism of his historical assertions, his work remains a foundational creation that granted Kabbalah academic legitimacy in the modern world and profoundly influenced Western thought and various spiritual movements.

The Religious Philosophy of the Hebrews: A Comprehensive Study of the Thought, Research Methodology, and Revolutionary Claims of Adolf Franck in His Book "Kabbalah"

Adolf Franck's book, "La Kabbale, ou la philosophie religieuse des Hébreux" (Kabbalah, or the Religious Philosophy of the Hebrews), first published in Paris in 1843, is considered one of the most foundational and influential works in the modern historiography of Jewish mysticism.[1, 2] Franck, who was the first Jewish philosopher in France to achieve the lofty academic status of "Agrégation" and who served as professor at the Collège de France, sought in this book to rescue Kabbalah from the depths of oblivion and contempt that characterized the attitude of nineteenth-century maskilim toward mysticism.[2, 3, 4] Franck's central claims undermined the prevailing conception of his time, which viewed Kabbalah as a collection of superstitious beliefs or a late forgery, and presented it as a profound, consistent, and fundamentally rational philosophical system that grants man the highest status in the history of religious and philosophical thought.[1, 3, 5]

The Historical and Intellectual Background of the Book's Composition

To understand Franck's claims, one must grasp the historical context in which he operated. In the first half of the nineteenth century, Western European Jewry, and especially French Jewry, was in the midst of an accelerated process of emancipation. Jews sought to integrate into general society as individuals with rights, while defining their Judaism as a "religion" rather than as a "mystical community" or "nation."[3] Within this framework, rationalist currents in Judaism, identified with the Wissenschaft des Judentums movement, tended to marginalize or reject Kabbalah as a foreign, obscure, and irrational element that damaged the enlightened image of the modern Jew.[3, 6]

Franck positioned himself against this tendency. He argued that Kabbalah is not "thaumaturgical hugger mugger," but rather an enlightened and sophisticated philosophy capable of teaching even the most advanced cultures the distinction between knowledge and wisdom.[3] His book was the first to make Kabbalah accessible and comprehensible to the educated European public, while employing a rigorous comparative philosophical methodology.[1, 7]

Milestones in Adolf Franck's Life and the Publication of His Book

Franck's Methodology: Victor Cousin's Eclecticism and Kabbalah

Franck was profoundly influenced by his teacher and patron, Victor Cousin, father of the eclectic current in French philosophy.[4] Cousin maintained that truth is dispersed among different philosophical systems throughout history, and the researcher's task is to synthesize the positive and eternal components within them.[4] Franck applied this approach to Kabbalah, viewing it as an expression of the "human spirit" in its struggle to understand the divine.[4]

This methodology led Franck to examine Kabbalah not as an isolated revelation, but as part of a continuum of collective ideational development.[4] He did not separate philosophy from its history, and argued that understanding the kabbalistic system requires analysis of the historical roots and reciprocal influences with Eastern and Western cultures.[4] This approach enabled him to present Kabbalah as a vital component in the "history of human thought" rather than as an ethnic curiosity.[11]

Analysis of the Foundational Texts: Sefer Yetzirah and Sefer ha-Zohar

At the center of Franck's research stands a meticulous analysis of the two fundamental texts of Kabbalah: Sefer Yetzirah and Sefer ha-Zohar. Franck dedicates extensive chapters to the internal analysis of these books, while attempting to prove their essential antiquity.[1, 12]

Sefer Yetzirah: The Metaphysics of Language and Numbers

Franck views Sefer Yetzirah as the most ancient foundation of speculative Kabbalah. He argues that the book does not deal with primitive cosmology but rather presents a sophisticated philosophical system in which language and mathematics are the building blocks of reality.[1, 13] He analyzes the concept of thirty-two wondrous paths of wisdom, which include the ten sefirot (ideal numbers) and the twenty-two fundamental letters.[14, 15] Franck argues that the sefirot in Sefer Yetzirah are not magical entities but rather metaphysical principles representing the "spirit of the living God," air, water and fire, and the six directions of space.[14, 15] Franck's central claim regarding Sefer Yetzirah is that the system described in it lays the foundation for the conception of emanation, in which the world is created through the gradual embodiment of the divine spirit in matter, and not through arbitrary creation of "something from nothing" in the classical sense.[14, 15]

Sefer ha-Zohar: The Anatomy of the Divine and the World

Sefer ha-Zohar constitutes for Franck the universal codex of Kabbalah. Contrary to the criticism of his contemporaries, Franck argued that the Zohar is not a modern thirteenth-century creation, but rather preserves an ancient core of oral traditions attributed to Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai and his companions.[11] Franck analyzes the Zohar through three principal prisms:

The Allegorical Method: The Zohar views Scripture as merely a "garment" for hidden truth. Franck argues that this hermeneutic approach attests to an attempt to liberate the spirit from the constraints of the literal text.[11, 12]

The Nature of the Divine: Franck emphasizes the concept of Ein Sof as the center of Zoharic thought, representing God before He assumed form or attribute.[15, 16]

The Structure of the Universe: The description of the different worlds and the relationship between them as a single organic fabric in which "all is one."[15]

The Claim of Antiquity and the Historical Polemic

One of Franck's most central and influential claims is that the kabbalistic system developed long before its official publication in the Middle Ages. Franck uses internal evidence from the Talmud and midrashim to prove that kabbalistic concepts such as "ma'aseh bereshit" and "ma'aseh merkavah" already contained the seeds of the Zoharic system.[3]

Franck argues that the fact that the Mishnah (Ḥagigah 2a) imposes severe restrictions on the study of the secrets of creation and the chariot attests to the existence of a developed esoteric teaching already in the tannaitic period.[3] He maintains that this teaching was transmitted secretly among a select group of sages, and that Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai was the central figure who shaped the core of what would later become Sefer ha-Zohar.[11] Although Franck admits that later editing may have occurred in the thirteenth century, he insists that the metaphysical ideas are ancient and cannot be the product of a single author's invention in the medieval period.[7, 11]

Comparison of Positions Regarding the Antiquity of the Zohar

The Philosophical Core: Ein Sof, Sefirot, and Emanation

Franck presents Kabbalah as a complete metaphysical system attempting to solve the question of the relationship between the absolute (God) and the finite (the world). His claim is that Kabbalah offers a solution that combines transcendence with immanence.[15]

Ein Sof and the Concept of "Ayin"

According to Franck, the divine in its highest degree is "Ein Sof"—a state of absolute perfection, boundless and indefinable.[16, 21] He emphasizes a profound point in kabbalistic analysis: the term "Ayin" used to describe Keter or Ein Sof does not signify emptiness but rather "the absence of limitation."[15] No name can be attributed to God,
Title or action before the commencement of emanation, for every name constitutes a limitation, and God is the Absolute Infinite.[16, 21]

The Ten Sefirot as Vessels of Manifestation

The ten sefirot are, according to Franck, the vessels or "measures" through which the Infinite Light contracts itself in order to enable the existence of the world.[15, 21] Franck describes the sefirot as a gradual process of "condensation" of the spirit:

The circularity of the sefirot: they are held in the Infinite as coal is held in flame.[15]

Adam Qadmon: Franck sees in this concept the ideal model of the universe, in which the ten sefirot reflect the spiritual form of the Primordial Man.[15]

Unity within Multiplicity: Despite there being ten sefirot, Franck emphasizes the kabbalistic assertion that "All is One." The sefirot are not separate from God but are the ways in which He reveals Himself to His creatures.[15]

The Anthropology of Kabbalah: Man as the Center of the Universe

One of the most famous claims in Franck's book is that no other doctrine in the history of philosophy or religion has granted man a higher rank than Kabbalah.[1, 7] Man, according to Franck, is not merely a creature created "in the image," but is tantamount to "a divine presence upon the earth."[1]

Franck analyzes the structure of the kabbalistic soul and shows how it reflects the structure of the supernal sefirot. He emphasizes the concept of "Adam Qadmon" and explains that the human form (the head, arms, body, and legs) corresponds to the letters of the Tetragrammaton (YHWH) when written vertically.[15] His central claims regarding the soul include:

Divine Origin: The soul is a part of God from above, and it existed before its descent into the body in the spiritual world.[15]

Exalted Purpose: Man's role is to elevate the world back to its divine source through his deeds and spiritual understanding.[15, 22]

The Doctrine of Transmigration: Franck sees in the transmigration of souls proof of divine compassion, which enables every soul to complete its repair (tiqqun) and achieve its final perfection in union with the Absolute.[15, 23]

Comparative Study: Kabbalah versus World Philosophy

Franck devotes a considerable portion of his book to comparing Kabbalah with other systems of thought, with the aim of isolating its unique sources. He examines the relationship between Kabbalah and Platonism, Neoplatonism, Gnosticism, and Philo of Alexandria.[1, 10, 12]

Kabbalah versus Plato and Plotinus

Franck identifies lines of similarity between Plato's theory of Ideas and the world of the sefirot, and between Plotinus's concept of "the One" and the Ein Sof.[1, 24] However, he argues that Kabbalah differs from them in that it is not dualistic. While among the Greeks there sometimes exists a sharp separation between "evil" matter and "good" spirit, Kabbalah sees matter as a low and condensed stage of the divine spirit itself.[15]

Kabbalah and Gnosticism

In contrast to scholars who saw Kabbalah as a type of Jewish Gnosticism, Franck argues that Kabbalah succeeded in avoiding the errors of the Gnostics. Gnosticism presented the creator of the world (the Demiurge) as an inferior or evil god, whereas Kabbalah preserves the unity of God and explains the existence of judgment and rigor (din and gevurah) as a necessary part of the divine balance.[15, 25]

The Revolutionary Thesis: The Zoroastrian Source and Persian Influence

This is the central and most controversial claim in Franck's book: he concludes that the deepest source of the philosophical concepts of Kabbalah is found in the Zoroastrian religion of ancient Persia.[1, 9, 12]

Franck conducts a "process of elimination" in which he rules out Greek, Egyptian, and Christian sources as primary origins for Kabbalah, and points to the Babylonian Exile (c. 500 BCE) as the decisive period in which the sages of Israel were exposed to the teachings of Zarathustra.[1, 9, 26] He argues that during this period Zarathustra was active in the same geographical region, and the encounter between Hebrew monotheism and Persian metaphysics gave birth to the kabbalistic foundations.[1, 9]

Parallels between Kabbalah and Zoroastrianism according to Adolphe Franck

Franck argues that the Jews did not "steal" these ideas, but rather "reconceptualized" them within the monotheistic framework of the Torah, thereby transforming Persian mythology into profound Jewish philosophy.[1, 5]

Adolphe Franck's Influence on Occultism and Western Thought

Paradoxically, Franck's book, which was written as a rational academic treatise, became one of the most important sources for the movements of Western occultism and esotericism in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.[29, 30, 31]

Éliphas Lévi, the father of modern French occultism, was profoundly influenced by Franck's presentation of Kabbalah as an ancient universal wisdom.[29, 30] Lévi adopted the idea that Kabbalah is "the key to all mysteries" and integrated the concepts of the sefirot with Tarot cards and ritual magic.[29] Movements such as the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn and Helena Blavatsky's Theosophical Society also relied on Franck's research to establish their claims regarding the existence of a "hidden tradition" common to all religions.[27, 29, 32]

For these audiences, Franck was not merely a scholar, but one who "decoded" Kabbalah and transformed it from a closed Jewish system into a broad esoteric philosophy capable of explaining the structure of the universe to every person.[1, 7, 22]

Modern Criticism: From Franck to Gershom Scholem

Despite his historical importance, Franck's claims came under sharp criticism from later academic research, headed by Gershom Scholem. Scholem, who revolutionized the study of Jewish mysticism in the twentieth century, appreciated Franck as one who opened the gate to scientific research, but rejected many of his conclusions.[3, 6, 33]

Scholem criticized Franck's tendency (and that of other nineteenth-century scholars) to see Kabbalah as an overly "enlightened philosophy." He argued that Franck attempted to "domesticate" Kabbalah and transform it into a clean rational system, while ignoring the mythic, demonic, and irrational elements that are at the heart of the Jewish mystical experience.[6, 25, 33]

Regarding the Zoroastrian thesis, Scholem argued that it lacked a solid philological and historical basis. He maintained that medieval Kabbalah (and especially the Sefer ha-Zohar) developed as a result of internal processes within the Judaism of southern France and Spain, arising from polemic with Aristotelian philosophy and Maimonides, and not as a direct inheritance from the Babylonian Exile.[29, 34] Scholem proved that the Zohar is a work of the thirteenth century, thereby refuting one of Franck's central claims regarding the antiquity of the text.[6, 17, 20]

Nevertheless, contemporary research (such as that of Boaz Huss) indicates that Franck's paradigm—which saw Kabbalah as a universal wisdom intersecting with other cultures—is what enabled Kabbalah to become a global cultural phenomenon in the modern era.[23, 30, 31]

Summary and Conclusions: The Book's Enduring Significance

Adolphe Franck succeeded in his original mission: he transformed Kabbalah into a subject worthy of profound philosophical and historical research.[1, 4] His claims, even if some of them were refuted by later philological research, raised fundamental questions that continue to occupy the world of thought to this day:

The Universalism of Kabbalah: Is Kabbalah a closed Jewish creation or is it an expression of a broader human wisdom that was influenced by the East?[1, 9]

The Status of Man: The kabbalistic conception of man as the center of creation and as a partner to divinity remains one of the most influential ideas on religious humanism.[1, 7]

The Relationship between Rationality and Mysticism: Franck demonstrated that mysticism is not necessarily the enemy of reason, but rather can be a structured and coherent philosophical system.[3]

Franck's book remains an essential text for anyone seeking to understand the way in which Jewish thought met modernity. He did not merely explain Kabbalah; he granted it "the right to exist" in the enlightened world, and thereby paved the way for the great flourishing of engagement with Jewish spirituality in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.[1, 5, 22]
